strings.name: Samantha Power
strings.role: Harvard professor, former US ambassador to the UN and USAID administrator
strings.summary: Samantha Power is an American foreign-policy practitioner, author and teacher. After reporting on the wars in the former Yugoslavia, she won a Pulitzer Prize for her study of US responses to genocide. In the Obama administration she worked on multilateral affairs and human rights before becoming UN ambassador. She led USAID from 2021 to 2025, then returned to Harvard. Her career connects public advocacy, government decisions and international aid, including the institutional constraints on humanitarian goals.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 18 November 2026. Harvard’s faculty directory and return announcements establish her current role; historical government biographies are read in their original context. Only the confirmed birth year, 1970, is used. Reporting from September 2026 supports recent public activity.
strings.influence.rationale: She served as US ambassador to the United Nations and led an international development agency, with longstanding involvement in human rights, humanitarian assistance and foreign policy.
strings.facts.f1.label: Education and migration
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in 1970, she moved from Ireland to the United States at nine. She earned a Yale BA in 1992 and a Harvard JD in 1999; the JD is a professional law degree, distinct from a research doctorate. Her subsequent career has spanned university teaching, writing and public service.
strings.facts.f2.label: University posts and government terms
strings.facts.f2.value: She is Harvard Law School’s William D. Zabel Professor of Practice in Human Rights and the Kennedy School’s Anna Lindh Professor of the Practice of Global Leadership and Public Policy. UN ambassador and USAID administrator are former roles; her professorship does not mean she still represents the US government.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Humanitarian access during crisis
strings.highlights.h1.text: At the Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing on 10 April 2024, Power shared concerns about the severe risk of famine in Gaza, discussing child malnutrition and the urgent need for greater aid access. This records her testimony at that time; risk assessments, relief measures and actual outcomes require separate evaluation.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Public advocacy after government service
strings.highlights.h2.text: In September 2026, she spoke at the Clinton Global Initiative about how a partnership to prevent childhood lead poisoning continued after US aid cuts. Reporting confirms an actual address; cooperation and funding pledges do not establish that lead exposure has ended or every aid shortfall has been filled.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Returns to a joint Harvard appointment
strings.timeline.t1.text: After her USAID term, she returned to the Law and Kennedy Schools to resume teaching and public-policy work. The announcement came on 16 May; Harvard’s July retrospective confirmed her return on 1 June. Her previous joint appointment ran from 2017 to 2021.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Sworn in as USAID administrator
strings.timeline.t2.text: She became the 19th administrator of the US Agency for International Development in the Biden administration, leading the development and humanitarian-assistance agency until 2025. Its programmes involve many implementing partners, so all aid outcomes cannot be attributed to one person.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Publishes The Education of an Idealist
strings.timeline.t3.text: Her memoir, The Education of an Idealist: A Memoir, recounts her movement from journalism and academia into government. It offers her own perspective and is a different kind of evidence from an independent policy evaluation.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Presents credentials at the United Nations
strings.timeline.t4.text: The Senate confirmed her on 1 August by 87 votes to 10; appointment followed on 2 August and presentation of credentials on 5 August. State Department historical records give 21 January 2017 as the mission’s termination. The three entry dates correspond to distinct procedures.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Joins the White House National Security Council
strings.timeline.t5.text: She served in the Obama administration as special assistant to the president and senior director for multilateral affairs and human rights until 2013, then became UN ambassador. This was a White House policy-coordination post, distinct from employment by a UN institution.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Wins the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction
strings.timeline.t6.text: She won for A Problem from Hell: America and the Age of Genocide, published in 2002, a study of US responses to genocide. The book examines American policy choices and inaction in the face of mass atrocities abroad.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Earns a Harvard professional law degree
strings.timeline.t7.text: She completed Harvard Law School’s JD while moving into human-rights policy research and teaching. She also served as founding executive director of the Carr Center for Human Rights Policy, bringing concerns developed through war reporting into policy research.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Begins reporting on the former Yugoslav wars
strings.timeline.t8.text: From 1993 to 1996 she reported on the wars in the former Yugoslavia for several publications. Her experience as a war correspondent preceded government service and provided an important background to her later work on human rights and foreign policy.
